# My LLM sessions were confusing me, so I built with-my-dashboards

How AI streamlined my digital life

## Build your own web server

My road to a more productive digital life started when I asked Claude Code (CC) to build a web server for me. It's called with-my-dashboards (WMD), a full-stack web application in a single file that has grown into the control panel for my whole desktop. Its generic core is on GitHub , for you to build your own on.

It started with reading. Long answers are hard to read inside CC, so I ask it to write them to a markdown file and open that in the browser. CC can do that by itself. What it can't choose is where the page turns up, and that's the problem WMD solved: I wanted every page in a known browser window, on the workspace I'm currently on.

It has grown since then. A "personal agent", one that goes off and does things for you while you're not there, isn't something I want. But I do like the convenience such agents promise, and WMD is a big part of how I get it. Anything I find myself doing a lot gets streamlined. Sometimes that's a small ~/bin command, sometimes a button or page in WMD, and sometimes just a rule CC follows for me, such as always backing up a file before changing it.

When I start WMD from the command line, it opens several browser windows, each with many tabs. I have three areas of focus at the moment, so I work across three workspaces. The one step I haven't been able to automate is moving each window to its workspace, but that only takes a few seconds.

About the videos: they're screen recordings, made when WMD was still called mdserve, and the text in them is small. Open a panel, then go full screen before you press play. YouTube picks the picture quality from the size of the player, so a small player gets a blurry picture.

## Everything lives on a tab

As you saw in the video, I start WMD from workspace 2. That's the workspace I use for control, and for anything that isn't a programming project. The idea is that WMD bootstraps the machine. After that, all the work I need to do is on a WMD browser tab somewhere.

When I want to work on WMD itself, I start a new CC session and ask it to read WMD.md , where its documentation lives. If you haven't worked with CC, or a similar coding agent such as Codex CLI or Gemini CLI: maintenance documents like this are written by the AI itself, from the conversations you have with it at its prompt.

Browser tabs are just URLs. On startup WMD reads them from an EDN file, and that file gets changed during my conversations with CC.

A tab gets there in one of three ways:

- Always wanted. These are often complete programs, such as the dashboards for my projects, or ordinary sites such as Gmail and Slack, and they come back every time WMD starts.

- Asked for. I've asked CC to "put it up". This is usually markdown documentation.

- Opened by another tab. A button on another tab was pressed, usually to take a closer look at something, such as a log.

Each tab also gets a coloured dot as its icon, so I can tell at a glance what kind of tab it is. Ordinary websites keep their own icons, but they're just as much part of WMD: remembered and reopened with the rest, and CC can put one up in the correct window as easily as a document. The idea is to keep it down to one browser window per workspace.

## Sessions

I often have more than a dozen CC sessions open, each in a terminal tab on its project's workspace. The Sessions tab lists that workspace's sessions, one row each: its title, a line on what it's doing now, and how full its context is. Each row also shows whether the session is busy, idle or waiting for me.

## More features, and your own Windows Explorer

The video on improving WMD showed "Refresh" for how much memory is in use, and "Remember Tabs", which saves the open tabs.

One rule Claude follows for me is to always make a backup before changing a markdown file. That makes a mess of backup files, which of course can be tidied up.

The next video shows the tidying up.

Imagine having your own programmable version of Windows Explorer per workspace. You just saw that in the video above ! There's always at least one of these tabs in each workspace. The video doesn't show it, but clicking a file opens a new tab that displays that type of file. Markdown files matter most, so they're listed with the most recently changed first.

Many of WMD's buttons don't do the work themselves. They run a small command from my ~/bin directory, the same command I could type at a shell prompt, or that CC can run for me. The "Flotsam" button in the video runs archive-flotsam , a script that moves backup files and screenshots into a timestamped archive folder. Most of the commands behind buttons are just a few lines of bash. A few buttons, such as the memory "Refresh" and "Remember Tabs", are built into WMD itself.

## Fewer terminals

Working as a developer or a support person, you end up with terminals everywhere, some temporary and some running permanently, and they clutter your desktop. There are plenty of ways to organise them: tmux or its newer cousin Zellij, tiling window managers such as i3, and on macOS, iTerm2, or cmux , which is built for running several coding agents at once.

The terminals that cluttered my desktop were mostly long-running processes: web servers, build watchers and the like. Those now run in the background, each terminal having been replaced by a row of buttons ("Launch", "Stop" and "Log") on a dashboard tab, one at a time or a whole group at once. "Log" opens the output in another tab, which I close when I'm done. All I keep is one tabbed terminal window per workspace, for my CC sessions and the occasional one-off terminal session.

Tools like tmux and i3 arrange terminals, while WMD removes the need for them, and it solves two problems along the way. One is proximity: the controls sit on a tab in the same window as the docs, dashboards and logs I'm working with. The other is customisation. A general-purpose tool gives everyone the same thing, so it fits nobody exactly. Whereas every button on my dashboards is one I asked CC for, grouped the way I work.

## Use runbooks

That occasional one-off terminal session I mentioned is often a runbook, often on another machine.

Some jobs need me, rather than CC, to type the commands, because they need my password or a console. For those, CC writes a runbook: a plain file of shell commands, with comments saying why each step is there. I press Ctrl-x n and the next step appears at my prompt, already typed, and nothing runs until I press Enter. No more copying commands out of the chat. The tool is called cmdq, and it's a gist you can install in a minute.

Each step's output is saved for CC to read back, and my place is saved too, so a job can span reboots. When the job is on another machine, CC copies the runbook there, and I log in and keep pressing Ctrl-x n. Each runbook is a dated file kept with its output, so there's a history of what ran on each machine.

## Complex deployment

Buttons aren't only for small jobs. Our point-of-sale system (POSES) is five webapps (chat, till, prods, custs and pos) that run on one production server, and deploying them is a job with several steps. It now lives in WMD in a Deploy panel on the POSES dashboard tab, as five buttons in the order they're used:

- Plan compares what's live with the latest code (whether committed or not), app by app, and shows what a deploy would ship.

- Ship builds and uploads an uberjar for each changed app, stopping at the first failure.

- Release doesn't actually do anything! Instead, it prints the step for the human deployer to run on the server.

- Record checks that every app that was shipped is really live, and fails loudly if one isn't, which catches a step missed on the server. It then notes what went live, so the next Plan can work from that note instead of having to query the live server. It's also the only way Plan knows which version of the shared library is in production, because the server doesn't say.

- Confirm runs the plan again, read-only, and should find nothing left to deploy. Its log ends: "Confirm done. If every app above shows 'up-to-date', the deploy is complete." It then restarts the development build watchers that Ship had to stop.

Each step has a coloured dot showing whether it has run and how it went, and a "Log" button for its output.

Five repos plus a shared library is a polyrepo , and polyrepos have a reputation: each extra repo is one more thing to start, keep in step and deploy. The POSES tab takes care of all three:

- Running them together. One page shows every app, each with its own Start, Stop, Restart and Log buttons, and "Start all" starts the lot. What each app needs, such as the database, is shown beside it, and shared services have their own row.

- One address. On my development machine, Caddy puts all the apps behind one address, the way the web server in production does. So development behaves like the real system, with the apps running side by side rather than on scattered ports.

- Deploying them. The Deploy panel works out, repo by repo, what needs shipping, and keeps track of which version of the shared library is live.

So I no longer hesitate to start a new repo.

## Life hacks

The same habit works away from the desk. Five examples, and how each one works.

Reading on the couch. When I say "put it up on the tab", CC adds a document to a reading list, which a second, deliberately tiny web server shows on my tablet. That server can only show the list and the documents on it. WMD itself only listens on the machine's own internal address , so nothing on the LAN can reach it. The terminal and editor pages simply don't exist on the tablet's server, so nothing I add to WMD later can leak onto the network by accident. A web page can go on the list too; it's just a link to the real site.

The big screen. "Put it on the big screen" sends a page to the TV, where it waits for the next time I sit down to read. Behind that phrase is bigscreen , a small command on my desktop: give it a web address and the page goes to the TV. CC runs it when I ask, and I can type it myself too. The TV is really just an HDMI screen for a spare Linux machine, which I call the media machine. That beats a smart TV: the media machine is a normal computer, so it can run a web server and a fully controllable Chrome. A page on the TV is no use if you can't scroll it from the couch, so the media machine runs its own little web server, tvremote , and my phone is the remote control. In reading mode it scrolls the page up and down, makes the text bigger or smaller, reloads it, and plays the page's YouTube videos; the same remote also does Netflix. tvremote shows pages in a separate Chrome with its own profile, because Chrome won't let a program take control of your everyday one. It's on GitHub if you have a spare machine and a TV.

What makes tvremote work is the same trick WMD uses, but on two devices. In WMD, the page I click on and the browser being driven are one and the same: a button on the page asks WMD, and WMD drives that browser. With tvremote there are two browsers: the phone's browser, and Chrome on the media machine. One web server sits between them. When I press a button on the phone's browser, the press goes over the Wi-Fi to tvremote (the web server on the media machine). tvremote and that Chrome both run on the media machine, so tvremote can drive it directly. Thus a press goes from browser, to web server, to browser. In a way, Chrome on the media machine is acting as a web server too, taking commands from tvremote. The phone's browser has no power over the TV at all; it can only ask a web server that has. Any device on the LAN can be the remote, and bigscreen on my desktop is just one more of them.
